Price, Kenneth Fred · Prime 3 A life · 1921–1960 · Edna · Pittsburg · Neodesha, Kansas

Kenneth Fred Price
Paratrooper, 1942–1943

↑² MM— paternal grandfather of Brent (the anchor of this page)

Kenneth Fred Price was born on August 4, 1921, at Edna, Kansas, the second son of Louie Edwin Price and Ruth Winifred Pearson. He was a paratrooper in the Second World War and was wounded in Sicily in July 1943. He died at home in Neodesha, Kansas, on September 2, 1960, aged thirty-nine. He is Brent's paternal grandfather; Brent never met him.

Edna Pittsburg Three years before the war Camp Wolters The marriage Staging Sicily The hospitals Home September 1960 Shirley's fight The map Open questions Notes

Edna, August 1921

He was born on Thursday, August 4, 1921, at Edna, in Labette County, Kansas.1 Proven The day was unsettled, with rain general across the eastern half of the state, fair and cooler by nightfall.

The local paper, a week late the way small papers were, ran the item among the week's overlooked news: "One of the several items overlooked last week, was the arrival of a fine, big boy at the home of Mr. and Mrs. Louie Price of south Edna." No name, no date. Just the boy, the parents, and the south side of town, where Louie Price worked as a section foreman on the Missouri Pacific.

He was the second son of Louie Edwin Price and Ruth Winifred Pearson. They called him Kenneth Fred.

Pittsburg

By March 1925 the family had moved northwest to rural Lincoln Township, Crawford County. Kenneth was three on the Kansas state census, in a rented house on rural route R6. His father worked the railroad as a signal man. His grandfather C. B. Pearson was in the household.

Then Louie died — 1926 — and by April 1930 the census finds Ruth heading a rented household at 210 Thirteenth Street, Pittsburg: ten dollars a month, sons Conrad ten, Kenneth eight, Louie seven, Carroll five, all in school. The enumerator wrote the boys' father's birthplace as "At Sea."2 Two older men boarded with them: Marion C. Osborn, fifty-eight, a railroad flagman, listed as "Father," and Charles C. Pearson, fifty-seven.

Pittsburg held him through the Depression. He was a sophomore in the 1938 high-school yearbook and "Student" in the 1942 city directory. On February 16, 1942, aged twenty, he registered for the draft in Pittsburg — born August 4, 1921, at Edna, Kansas; next of kin his mother, Ruth Price.

Three years before the war

Visiting the Neodesha news office after his discharge, Kenneth told the paper he had "served three years in the army before the war and enlisted the second time May 9, 1942." It stands here as his own reported history.3 Open

If it is true, he was already a soldier when the country went to war, before he was a husband or a father. No record of a first enlistment has surfaced.

Camp Wolters

On May 9, 1942, he enlisted at Fort Leavenworth: Private, in the Army of the United States.4 Basic training took him to Camp Wolters in Palo Pinto County, Texas, an infantry replacement training center at Mineral Wells.

The family, asked in 2026 how to describe his service, put it in one line: he was infantry that was training jumping. The wedding notice that summer already called him a member of the parachute battalion at Camp Wolters.

The marriage

Shirley Lee Edwards of Neodesha met Kenneth during the war, in a class her father taught — something to do with machines for the war effort. She quit school in her senior year, and went to Texas and got married.8 The family story adds that he went absent without leave to do it — twelve weeks into his service, slipping away from a training camp to reach a wedding.6

They married at nine o'clock on Saturday night, August 1, 1942, at Palo Pinto, Texas, the Reverend Walker of the Christian church reading the vows.7 Proven The Neodesha paper spelled the town "Polo Pinto," twice, in its own hand. The notice said the couple would make their home at Mineral Wells for the present, and added that Mrs. Price had lived in Neodesha most of her life and received her education in the Neodesha schools. It was a scorching north-Texas Saturday — 99 degrees at the top of the afternoon, 76 overnight, no rain.

Staging

By April 1943 the Neodesha paper has him home on a three-week furlough — styled a technical sergeant, stationed at Shenango Valley, Pennsylvania, a personnel replacement depot — with his wife, "the former Shirley Edwards."9 In mid-June, word reached Neodesha that he had "arrived safely somewhere in England."

Sicily

He was a paratrooper of the 504th Parachute Infantry Regiment, 82nd Airborne Division.10 Probable The regiment jumped into Sicily on the night of July 11, 1943, and fought across the island in hundred-degree heat.

The family tells the wounding this way: on his first jump, he was shot while parachuting down, and he lay in the mud behind enemy lines until he was found. The home paper, that December, told it plainly: "He lost all his fingers on the left hand by a German machine gun during fighting behind the enemy lines where he landed by parachute with other members of his company."11

The hospitals, and the coding

"Kenneth has been in a hospital in England since the latter part of July," the home paper wrote, "recovering from wounds received in the invasion of Sicily." Then O'Reilly General Hospital in Springfield, Missouri: "Pvt. Kenneth F. Price has arrived from overseas and is now in O'Reilly General Hospital in Springfield, Mo.… He expects to be home in a few weeks." His name stands on the hospital's morning report for December 9, 1943, among twenty-five sick men attached unassigned, to be discharged.12

On December 9, 1943, he was discharged for disability. The hospital card that codes his wound — a bullet wound to the fingers of his left hand, taken in July 1943 — codes the discharge "not in line of duty (existed prior to service)."13 A bullet wound, coded as if it had happened before he ever served. The family kept his Purple Heart for decades, until it was stolen.14

Home

He and Shirley had moved to Neodesha in 1943, and he made Wilson County his. A daughter, Sharon Lou, was born in Neodesha Township on December 9, 1944; Kenneth Lee followed. The 1950 census finds the household at 213 South 5th Street, Neodesha — Kenneth, 28, working forty hours a week as a burner at the Independent Plant; Shirley, 24, keeping house; Sharon, five; Kenneth Lee, three.15 Proven His obituary names his employer as the Continental Can Company at Coffeyville.

His in-laws lived across the street. Ira and Ruth Edwards — Shirley's parents — were at 224 South 5th Street, only a one-minute walk from his front door. In March 1951 the Neodesha paper caught the whole family at a surprise evening for Shirley's grandparents, C. C. and Grace Edwards, at their home at 609 Indiana Street — the couple's fifty-fifth wedding anniversary, with "Mrs. Kenneth Price, Mr. Price and children, Sharon and Kenny" named among the guests from across town.16

Aunt Dodie's notes remember those years in fragments: Kenny and Dodie sneaking their kid out to little-league games, camp meetings and Elk City and Neodesha porches. He was a member of the Christian church at Pittsburg, the town he had grown up in.

September 1960

He had been in poor health for the past year. In the early hours of Friday, September 2, 1960, he died in his sleep at home at 213 South 5th Street. The cause was listed as a heart attack. He was thirty-nine.17 Proven

The funeral was that Sunday afternoon at the William Fawcett Funeral Home, the Reverend Alvin Daetwiler officiating. A Neodesha National Guard platoon conducted the military graveside service; the flag was folded and presented to Shirley. Boy Scout Troop 28 attended in a body. He was buried in Neodesha Cemetery, in the family lot, beside where Shirley and her mother would later lie.18

In November 2013, a flower was left on his memorial page: "My grandfather that I never knew. Thank you for your service to your country and your family." — B Price. That was Brent.

Shirley's fight

Shirley fought the VA over his pension for the rest of her life. The family says his service records were sunk coming home from the war, and that two men with the same name had their records crossed and never fully fixed. With the wound coded "not in line of duty," the VA had every reason to say no, and she kept asking anyway.

Her sister's remembrance fills in the years the records leave blank. Shirley had never worked a day in her life, but "when Ken's pension and stuff got all fouled up she had to, to raise those new kids." She went to work as a butcher in a local grocery — she "didn't know one end of a pig from another," but she learned, and she was good. One day she fell at work and had to go on disability. After that she more or less looked after their mother. "She was the best mother to her kids," the remembrance says, "and when times were lean she would do without things for herself to make sure those kids had what they needed." Her own story is told on her page.

The map

Open questions

These are still open:

The VA claims file. Shirley's decades of claims, decisions, and appeals, and how the VA ruled on the "not in line of duty" coding year by year. The request package is prepared and in the family's hands.

His death certificate. The Kansas certificate would name the informant and state his age, his birth date, and the cause of death. An application is prepared and unfiled; his son Kenneth Lee may already hold a copy.

The Purple Heart's paper. The medal itself was in the family until it was stolen. The order or award card that issued it has not surfaced; a replacement request is prepared for Kenneth Lee to sign and mail.14

The training company, and the wedding. Camp Wolters morning reports for July and August 1942 would name his company, and they are where the absent-without-leave wedding story would be settled.

The second Kenneth Price. The separation research: find the other man in the Second World War records and uncross the two files for good.

The back of the jump wings. A sterling stamp and maker's marks would date the badge Brent holds.

Before 1950 in Neodesha. The family moved there in 1943; 213 South 5th Street is proven only from 1950. The earlier address is unplaced.

Notes

  1. The family's date — August 4, 1921 — is carried by his own draft registration, the 1925 Kansas census, the 1930 and 1940 censuses, his 1938 yearbook, and his 1960 obituary. The Army paperwork's 1917 belongs to the crossed records of a second same-named veteran; Brent ruled on October 2, 2026, that the 1917 chain is cross-contamination, and it is flagged wherever it appears in this story, never narrated as fact. The birth weather is the day-after weather box of the Coffeyville Daily Journal, Friday, August 5, 1921, p. 1: "Kansas — Unsettled this afternoon followed by generally fair tonight and Saturday; cooler tonight and in east and south portions Saturday," with rains "general throughout the eastern half of the state during the past twenty-four hours."
  2. The "At Sea" entry is the enumerator's hand, not the family's claim; a shipboard-birth legend for Louie's father attaches to it in the family's telling. Marion C. Osborn's "Father" is the census relation as written; whose father he was, the records do not say, and he is carried in the research as a household FAN, unproven.
  3. The claim is Kenneth's own, printed in the Neodesha paper's December 1943 telling of his wounding and recovery. No enlistment record, morning report, or discharge for a pre-war term has surfaced. The single ribbon bar visible in his Camp Wolters portrait is consistent texture, not proof.
  4. Service number 17057680. The enlistment face is the Army's record of May 9, 1942, Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.
  5. The photograph's kit dates and places it: summer khaki uniforms, M1923 cartridge belts, canvas leggings, M1903-pattern rifles, and no insignia on either man — an infantry replacement training center in the summer of 1942. The solo portrait's service coat, collar discs, single ribbon bar, and absence of chevrons read the same stateside training period; its large round shoulder patch matches no airborne division at this resolution and is not unit-identified. Both reads are from the October 30, 2026, photo investigation of the family's archive.
  6. The absence is Brent's family testimony. No disciplinary record has been found either way; the Camp Wolters morning reports are the named decider and have not been read for those weeks.
  7. The marriage's paper home is Palo Pinto County, Texas, August 1, 1942. The wedding weather is the Mineral Wells Index's day-after box: 99 degrees, 76 overnight, no rain.
  8. The meeting is told from the remembrance of Shirley's sister: "Shirley met Kenneth during the war — he was in a class their father taught, something to do with machines for the war effort. She quit school in her senior year and went to Palo Texas and got married." The sister was sorry she had not finished — Shirley "had a knack for design, a talent for clothes, and might have been a promising designer." The author is a sister of Shirley's, not confirmed by name; Dorene "Dodie" Edwards — later Mrs. Kenneth Hull of Independence — is confirmed as a sister on Brent's own tree material, but the authorship is not established. An earlier telling had Shirley in Texas visiting when they met; Brent ruled on October 30, 2026, that the visiting account carries no reference, and the remembrance's version is the story's.
  9. Neodesha News, April 15, 1943. The "T. Sgt." styling sits oddly against the trainee-to-discharge timeline — a private at discharge that December — and the Shenango Valley station matches the replacement-depot staging of that spring. The rank is carried as the paper's face, unresolved; the furlough and the station are the item's facts.
  10. The attribution rests on physical and timeline evidence: the jump-wings badge Brent holds is pinned to a blue-and-gold embroidered oval consistent with documented 504th PIR ovals, and the hospital card admits him in July 1943 in North Africa, the evacuation chain for the 504th's Sicily wounded. Company and battalion are unsourced. The rival face — "116th Infantry" — is falsified for July 1943 Sicily: the 116th was training in England and first saw combat at Omaha Beach in June 1944. The 116th line reaches Kenneth through the 1960 headstone application, an informant-supplied document in Shirley's hand, and through his family-sourced obituary, which calls him "a paratrooper in the 116th Infantry." Brent's ruling of October 2, 2026, assigns the 116th and 1917 matter to the crossed records.
  11. Two records disagree on the fingers, and both are carried: the paper says all of them; the Army hospital card says a bullet wound to the index and middle fingers of the left hand, with partial amputation; Brent's family testimony says two or three. The card is the clinical record. The dates compress too: the regiment jumped on the night of July 11, and the paper dates the wounding to July 25 — the family's "first jump" telling may fold the two into one.
  12. Headquarters Morning Report ending 2400, December 9, 1943; station O'Reilly General Hospital, Springfield, Missouri; organization "Patients 1763 SU." His roster row reads 17057680, Price, Pvt, under the remark "Above 25 EM sk hosp atchd unasgd to disch CDD" — sick in hospital, attached unassigned, to discharge on a certificate of disability for discharge. NARA Morning Reports, Roll 250, frame 1903; the only appearance of his service number in that roll's readable coverage.
  13. The card's disposition face reads: "Discharged for disability, not in line of duty (existed prior to service)," with the injury coded "not in line of duty: misconduct and all others." The card carries no unit field. A non-service-connected coding is what Shirley's pension fight ran against for thirty-five years.
  14. Brent's testimony, October 30, 2026: "We had the purple heart until it was stolen several decades ago." The award's paper — a general order or award card — is not in hand. A replacement packet (cover letter and SF 180) was prepared on October 30, 2026, for his son Kenneth Lee Price to sign and mail to the National Personnel Records Center, St. Louis. Under the Army's next-of-kin order, his eldest child, Sharon, stands first; the packet states the family structure openly, and any step involving her is Brent's call alone.
  15. 1950 census, Neodesha City, Wilson County, Kansas, ED 103-18, sheet 12, dwelling 128. The enumerator wrote the boy as "L. Kenneth" — first name an initial, middle name Kenneth; Brent's father confirms the boy is legally Kenneth Lee Price. The employer faces are carried together: the census image reads "Burner with Independent plant"; the obituary reads "employed at the Continental Can company at Coffeyville"; the family memorial says machinist. They are not merged.
  16. The anniversary item is the Neodesha News, March 5, 1951: a surprise evening at the home of C. C. (Cooper C.) Edwards and Grace (Jackson) Edwards, married March 5, 1896, at Oak Valley. The Kenneth family attended as guests of the household, not as its residents; 609 Indiana Street is about a six-minute walk from 213 South 5th. The 213/224 pair itself was verified on October 30, 2026, from the 1950 census sheet: dwellings 128 and 132 on the same sheet, opposite sides of the same block.
  17. Neodesha Register, September 8, 1960 — his obituary, supplied by the Kansas Historical Society. It gives his age as 39, born August 4, 1921, at Edna; married August 1, 1942, at Palo Pinto; moved to Neodesha in 1943; survived by Shirley, Kenneth, and Sharon of the home, his mother Ruth of Neodesha, and brothers Conrad of Texas, Louie of Los Angeles, and Carroll of Whittier.
  18. Neodesha Cemetery, 1st Addition, Block 6, Lot 975, Space 4; Shirley lies in Space 3, her mother Ruth T. Edwards in the same lot. The lot's exact point on the map is held open pending the cemetery office's verification, because the family's two marker points stand some 900 feet apart on the current map.
  19. The marker reads, verbatim: "KENNETH F. PRICE / KANSAS · WW II / PRIVATE 116TH INF REG / APRIL 4 1917 — SEPT. 2 1960." The inscription is the writing on Shirley's 1960 government-marker application. The 1917 date and the 116th line are the crossed-records face; see notes 1 and 10.
